title: American political coalitions contain cross-pressured value groups that a two-party split hides
source_unit: Pew Research Center 2026 Political Typology American Trends Panel survey and linked follow-up surveys

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel classified from 30 value and attitude questions

right_anchor_share.unit: percent of adults in the two highly ideological right-anchor groups

left_anchor_share.unit: percent of adults in the two highly ideological left-anchor groups

observations.method: Pew cluster analysis using 30 questions about government, economics, immigration, social values, national identity, and foreign policy; groups summarize patterned responses.
observations.uncertainty: Cluster assignments depend on the questions, model, cut points, and survey period. A group is not a fixed identity, a cause of behavior, or a forecast of future votes.
observations.subgroup: Nine Pew political typology groups with distinct party composition, values, demographics, and political attention.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-pressured views may reflect life stage, material position, identity, information, or local context rather than a stable coalition mechanism. Group size does not indicate political influence.

observations.period: November 17-30, 2025; within-coalition cultural and national-identity contrasts

denominator.unit: percent within each Pew political typology group

faith_first_conservatives_abortion_illeg.unit: percent saying abortion should be illegal in most or all cases

faith_first_christian_culture_important.unit: percent saying a culture based in Christian religious beliefs is very or extremely important to U.S. identity

observations.method: Descriptive within-typology comparison of cultural and national-identity attitudes.
observations.uncertainty: The group contrasts do not establish why groups differ or that typology membership causes issue positions. Religious-identity importance is not religious practice or constitutional preference.
observations.subgroup: Pew typology groups, including right-leaning groups with different cultural and institutional profiles.
observations.counterinterpretation: Party labels can hide meaningful disagreement within the same coalition; issue positions may also shift with context or question framing.

denominator.unit: percent of U.S. adults answering foreign-policy value questions

worlds_only_military_superpower_importan.unit: percent saying it is at least somewhat important for the U.S. to be the world's only military superpower

account_for_allies_interests.unit: percent saying the U.S. should consider allies' interests even when compromise is required

observations.method: Descriptive national foreign-policy value comparison within Pew's typology survey.
observations.uncertainty: These are stated preferences, not defense spending, alliance behavior, burden sharing, willingness to fight, or government decisions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and typology groups; support for power and alliance consideration can coexist within respondents and groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: A desire for military primacy does not necessarily reject alliances; a desire to consider allies does not establish willingness to bear cost or compromise.

related_sources.claim: Pew's public overview explains the nine-group typology and the 10,357-adult survey universe.

boundary: This record maps value-based coalition differences in a cluster-derived typology. It does not establish stable identities, causes of political behavior, turnout, vote choice, switching, policy influence, or a single center-versus-extremes mechanism.
